national.title: Shops looted as German cost of living protests turn violent
national.summary: The protests in cities across Germany - including Berlin, Hamburg and Frankfurt - came on the same day hundreds of thousands also protested in France.
national.body:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannons to disperse protesters targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.

The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.

On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.

Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.

Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.

Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".

national.title: How Gen Z Republicans running for Congress are thinking about the future of the party
national.summary: On the eve of what may prove to be a tough election for the GOP, young conservatives vying to be part of the first class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress want a role shaping the party's next chapter.
national.body:
In northeast Iowa, 29-year-old Joe Mitchell is vying to represent the state's second congressional district. It's a competitive race, one of just a handful considered to be a tossup , as voters sour on President Trump and Democrats see control of Congress as increasingly in reach.

Mitchell has the president's endorsement, and if he's successful, he would head to Washington D.C. next year as part of a new cohort: the first-ever class of Gen Z Republicans in Congress.

It wouldn't be a large class. Aside from Mitchell, just a handful of other Gen Z Republicans are in the running for House seats this fall. One is running in a reliably red district. The rest are longshots, vying for what's seen as safe blue seats.

While their numbers may be small, Mitchell says the idea of a new generation of leaders in Washington is something that voters have been responding to on the campaign trail.

"I think people are looking for hope, regardless of what party they're in," he said. "They want to see young people get involved, and I hear that everywhere we go."

Only on NPR Can I trust the polls? And other questions from listeners about the 2026 midterms The former state senator and real estate developer says his platform can speak to Iowans on both sides of the aisle. He's calling for term limits in the House, with a maximum of six terms, as well as a ban on congressional stock trading. He says he has also rejected campaign donations from corporate PACs.

It's all part of an "anti-corruption platform," a focus he says is uniquely rooted in his generation, as Americans under 30 report high levels of concern for their economic wellbeing and distrust of institutions.

"I just think that young people — on both sides of the aisle or no party affiliates — are frustrated with the system," he said. "They're frustrated and they should be."

national.title: Binance resumes withdrawals for some cryptocurrencies after heist
national.summary: The exchange said it would resume withdrawals in phases, pending security checks.
national.body: Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereal after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday."First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X.As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereal, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year."The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

national.summary: After Iran's Supreme Leader warned against restarting the war, President Trump suggested there are still targets to "take care of."
national.body: Iran warned on Sunday that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous conflict and that President Trump would not be the one to determine its duration. national.summary: Millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep this weekend when the time change commonly known as daylight saving ended for 2026, meaning clocks "fell back."
national.body: Millions of Americans gained an hour of sleep this weekend when the twice-a-year time change commonly known as daylight saving ended for 2026. In the fall and winter months, when the days are shorter, the U.S. returns to standard time, with daylight coming earlier in the morning.For example, in Boston on Saturday, before the time change, the sun rose at 7:16 a.m. and set at 5:39 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. On Sunday, back on standard time, sunrise will be at 6:17 a.m. and sunset will be at 4:37 p.m.The U.S. first adopted daylight saving time in 1918 during World War I as an effort to conserve fuel after Europe implemented its own time change, according to the Congressional Research Service. After the war, Congress repealed the clock switch but gave states the option to continue observing it.During World War II and the 1970s energy crisis, Congress brought year-round daylight saving time to the U.S., again with the goal of reducing energy consumption. national.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
national.summary: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
national.body:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.

The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

national.title: Trump thanks supporters for the memories in final campaign stops for 2026 midterms
national.summary: President Trump has maintained a near-daily rally schedule as Election Day draws closer, playing his greatest hits for loyal crowds in red states in what is a sort-of goodbye to campaigning.
national.body:
President Trump was comparing his 2016 campaign rally size to the rallies Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders was having that year, when the president took a detour.

"We have the biggest rallies ever in history," Trump said, turning from braggadocious to reflective. "I hope you enjoy it because you're never going to see it again. You will never see what we've done. You'll never see it happen again."

Trump was in South Carolina to boost two Senate candidates who he personally picked but who have struggled to ignite excitement among Republican voters: Darline Graham in South Carolina and Michael Whatley in North Carolina.

This was one of Trump's final rallies after a flurry of midterm campaign events over the past month. More than 25 rallies in October alone, mostly in red states where Republicans are facing serious political headwinds. The official purpose is to help those Republicans win their races, but for a president whose trademark has always been big raucous rallies, there was more to it.

Trump won't be on the ballot again and once these midterms are over, it's not clear how many Republican candidates will want voters pretending he is. Right now, though, that is his plea.

"Please pretend I'm on the ballot cause in a way I am on the ballot, because they want to do away with all of the tremendous things we've done. The tax cuts, the border," Trump said last week at a rally in Greenville, N.C.

Like any performer on what could be a farewell tour, Trump plays a lot of the greatest hits. He has a regular riff about tariffs.

"Tariffs. The tariffs. My favorite word," Trump said in Lubbock, Tex. "I always say it, but I had to change it to fifth favorite. You've heard me say this. I said it's my favorite word. It's made us rich."

national.title: Supreme Court hears religious freedom case centered on universal pre-K program
national.summary: The Archdiocese of Denver wants to be able to turn away LGBTQ families from Catholic preschools that receive state funding.
national.body:
On Tuesday, the Supreme Court hears arguments in a case that pits the Catholic Church against taxpayer funded school programs for all 4-year-olds in Colorado. At issue is whether religious schools may refuse to admit the children of gay and trans parents in violation of a state law that bars discrimination.

The first line of the Bill of Rights says: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof." As early as the founding of this country, Thomas Jefferson described the clause as creating a "wall of separation between church and state."

Law The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy The Supreme Court formally embraced that idea in the 1940s, making it the law of the land — until roughly 10 years ago. That's when the court's new conservative majority made an increasingly dramatic doctrinal U-turn, focusing not on the separation of church and state, but on that second clause in the First Amendment: protecting the free exercise of religion.

"It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago. It is just a complete shift," says Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch, who has written extensively about the Constitution's religion clauses.

To cite just one example, the Supreme Court, by an 8-to-1 vote, ruled in 1983 that that Bob Jones University should lose its tax exempt status because it prohibited interracial dating and interracial marriage on religious grounds, and that constitutes racial discrimination that the government money may not support.

That said, it's unclear if the court will reach a similar conclusion now.

Why is that? Because race has a "unique" place in U.S. history, contends professor Douglas Laycock, emeritus professor of law at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Virginia. "There's nothing like 250 years of slavery, civil war, 750,000 dead, three constitutional amendments. Nothing like that for any other group," he says.

Law Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case As for the Colorado case, Laycock acknowledges that the Denver archdiocese is discriminating, but he adds, "The question is whether that discrimination is a protected exercise of religion." Rather than focusing on separation of church and state, the current court instead has focused on the rights of religious groups when pitted against state and federal laws that ban discrimination based on race, sex, religion or other categories.

national.title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
national.summary: Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
national.body:
President Donald Trump walks from the podium after speaking at a campaign rally at the Ocean Center, in Daytona Beach, Fla., Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption

Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.

When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.

Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists.

The White House did not immediately react publicly to Saturday's dismissal or respond to an AP request for comment.

The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.

national.body: Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday, 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event.Klum was unrecognizable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits.The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand - specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band."I looked at my hand and I thought, 'Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,'" Klum said.The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume.In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, an 8-foot-tall (2.4-meter-tall) "Transformer," a werewolf from Michael Jackson's "Thriller" music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum-lookalikes, and Kali, the multiarmed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face."Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it," Klum said. "It's quite heavy."Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins."A little bit of Tom is with me," she said.

national.title: India's opposition holds mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
national.summary: It comes amid growing protests over a voter roll revision exercise feared to leave 130 million voters off rolls.
national.body:
Tens of thousands of people have gathered in India's capital Delhi for a major opposition rally demanding the resignation of the country's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.

The rally, organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, has brought together some of India's most prominent politicians at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi.

They arrived at the venue on Sunday after travelling in jeeps through crowds of cheering supporters.

Among those attending were Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, as well as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and Tejashwi Yadav.

The rally comes after weeks of opposition protests over a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from draft electoral rolls.

Opposition parties accuse chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of using the exercise to manipulate elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.

Protesters chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power", while others sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed around the venue, with barricades and traffic restrictions in place.

The Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support, though its leaders have yet to be seen at the event.

national.title: Democrats are used to heartbreak in Texas - could Talarico turn the tide?
national.summary: The state's $500m Senate race may be the most closely watched in the US midterms, and is about far more than control of Congress.
national.body:
North America correspondent Published 5 hours ago The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year – a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.

For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.

But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.

That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.

"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.

These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.

For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.

At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.

national.body: On the night of Feb. 25, 2023, outside Vanderbilt Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, Blaise Taylor was answering police questions about how a date turned into a medical emergency.BLAISE TAYLOR (police bodycam): We were together having a date night.Authorities wanted to know what happened to 24-year-old Jade Benning, who had been rushed to the hospital, arriving unresponsive.BLAISE TAYLOR (police bodycam): She started not to feel well.Jade Benning started that night with the hope of strengthening her relationship with Blaise Taylor, then a 26-year-old assistant football scout for the Tennessee Titans. Jade, a professional chef, was planning a special night at her apartment — cooking dinner, to be followed by painting pictures. But as the evening progressed, just minutes after taking selfies, Jade fell ill. Blaise said she was spitting up and shaking — unsure what to do, he first called his father.Evi Taylor, Blaise's mother, said their children would often contact their father, a college football coach, with medical questions. Like if somebody got hurt, he would be the first one there.Blaise Taylor calls 911Blaise's call with his dad lasted 30 seconds. national.title: Rioters loot stores in Germany amid cost of living protests
national.summary: After a largely peaceful protest, violence broke out between police and demonstrators in Germany.
national.body: Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing."We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education."At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.

A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight – and investors don't all like what they see.

Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.

These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.

They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.

Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.

Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".

On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them " a small component of the overall ecosystem , external " on CNBC.

Witch hunts reached their peak in England in the 1600s. In total across England and Scotland, around 5,000 women convicted of witchcraft were executed, some by hanging and some by burning."They were usually single women, spinsters, or widows, usually without a man to stick up for them," Claire Kehily, a member of the Maidstone Borough Council, told CBS News. "... They were easier to target." Inside Maidstone's town hall, Kehily showed CBS News a prison cell, reconstructed from an earlier medieval building where accused witches were held before trial.Now Kehily and her fellow councilors are lobbying the U.K. government and planning to petition King Charles III for an official pardon for all of Maidstone's convicted witches."It matters because it was a miscarriage of justice," Kehily said. "The crimes they were accused of they couldn't have been guilty of. And they had no way of being found innocent in many of the cases. This is 400 years ago. But there are still miscarriages of justice. There are still, to these days, people being scapegoated for things."America's most famous witch trials were in the 1690s in Salem, Massachusetts. Their memory was revived by Arthur Miller's play "The Crucible," an allegory for the political witch hunts led by Sen. Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s. national.summary: Defeat for Serbia's Aleksandar Vučiċ in last weekend's vote was a carbon copy of Viktor Orbán's fall in Hungary.
national.body:
When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučiċ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.

Both were ousted by popular movements - Orbán fell first, in April, defeated by Péter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.

The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.

But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.

Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.

Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.

During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.

A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.

local.summary: When everyone assumes somebody else will take responsibility, sometimes nobody does. There is an anonymous saying that captures this tendency to pass responsibility along: “This is a story about four people named Everybody, Somebody, Anybody, and Nobody. There was an important job to do, and Everybo
local.body:
Many facets of volunteering are pictured that include helping at events and fundraisers, art projects and helping get horses ready for riders.

When everyone assumes somebody else will take responsibility, sometimes nobody does.

There is an anonymous saying that captures this tendency to pass responsibility along: "This is a story about four people named Everybody, Somebody, Anybody, and Nobody. There was an important job to do, and Everybody was asked to do it. Everybody was sure Somebody would do it. Anybody could have done it, but Nobody did it. Somebody got angry because it was Everybody's job."

I have thought about those four people many times over the years. Lately, I have been thinking about them a lot.

When I visited my mother, I often helped her clean her house. One day, while clearing off her desk, I found three opened letters requesting donations. On each one, she had carefully recorded the check number, date, and amount she had contributed. Two were for monthly donations.

I asked her why she sent $30 every month to Save the Children. She explained that her contribution helped feed a child.

She understood something I needed to be reminded of: You don’t have to solve an entire problem to make a difference.

I work incredibly hard to raise the funds needed to keep Centaur Stride going. Many generous people help us, and I am deeply grateful for every one of them. But my mother was right about one thing: I had never directly asked her to contribute.

Mark Talley of Buffalo describes, in detail, his thinking about some of today’s youth. His mother, Geraldine Talley, was one of 10 people shot to d
local.body:
It’s not often that I will refer to another writer's thinking and observation of human behaviors in print. I am going to make an exception in this case. Mark Talley of Buffalo describes, in detail, his thinking about some of today's youth. His mother, Geraldine Talley, was one of 10 people shot to death by a white supremacist on May 14, 2022. He is also the author of "5/14 – the Day the Devil Came to Buffalo."

“My friends who are teachers see it every day. My other friends who are child psychologists who work at the office of Children and Family Services tell me that we are raising many children with no discipline, no accountability, no structure, and no responsibility. These thinking patterns are showing up in the work force and they are now impossible to ignore. We are raising a generation of kids that are not hire-able. A generation of "Mommy and Daddy kids" who say, "Please hold my hand" and who shut down the second life stops catering to them. In this day and age, and in this economy, that's a recipe for disaster. When we observe their lifestyle, factors such as no sleep, junk food, chemicals in everything we drink and eat, along with non-step stress. These factors hit motivation, confidence and behaviors. …

“Kids raised with all love and no limits appear to grow up with little resilience and no stress tolerance. They can talk about their feelings all day, but have great difficulty regulating them. Buffalo employers are observing it constantly – young adults who crumble under criticism, shut down when things get difficult and act like conflict is violence. Gentle parenting does not prevent trauma. It delays it. …

“Gentle parenting does not prepare Buffalo's young boys and girls for adulthood. It sets them up for collapse. We need to get back to parenting that mixes empathy with expectations, comfort with challenges, love with limits, or we are going to observe a generation who struggles under the weight of a world they were never taught to carry. Buffalo doesn't need harsher parents, just stronger ones.”

Mark has worked with many, many children in his lifetime. As you can read into his remarks, he obviously had a great mother that taught him values and not to ever quit and give up. He happens to be an African-American man in the inner city of Buffalo.

To think these problems are just inner-city problems is absurd. Many of you know me in this city as a teacher and basketball coach for more than 30 years. I apologize for nothing that I ever did when working with children, because I wasn't just teaching how to read or learn basketball, but taking these things into the future. Like Mark says, "When life hits you hard."

local.title: U.S. no longer keeps an open mind with elections
local.summary: This is the last weekend before the 2026 midterm elections. Most people have made up their minds already. Nevertheless, I’ll use this platform to express a few opinions about some recent controversies in an effort to urge people to think critically — logically and morally — and to vote for the candi
local.body:
This is the last weekend before the 2026 midterm elections. Most people have made up their minds already. Nevertheless, I'll use this platform to express a few opinions about some recent controversies in an effort to urge people to think critically -- logically and morally -- and to vote for the candidates who have the nation's best interest in their hearts and minds. While it's true that most people vote from their purses or wallets, I'd like to believe there is some idealism at play here. That there is an understanding of and belief in the Constitution, and a recognition of the importance of candidates’ character -- of their sense of decency and integrity.

There shouldn't be a debate over election security. Everyone agrees that citizens need to be legally registered in order to vote. Yet the controversy remains, despite overwhelming evidence that voter fraud is extremely rare. According to the American Bar Association, "Of the more than 25 million votes cast in six swing states in the 2020 election, an analysis by the Associated Press found fewer than 475 potential voter fraud cases, and even those cases were unconfirmed." Add to that the 59 local and federal courts who threw out alleged election fraud cases after the 2020 election.

Most importantly, we need to respect and appreciate those real people who work at the election sites. These are good, honest, everyday Americans performing a civic duty. They are democrats and republicans alike who, by and large, believe in free and fair elections. Hence, voter fraud should be a non-issue.

The controversy over the names of the candidates in the Alaskan Senate race is problematic. Allegedly, the campaign strategists for democrat candidate Mary Pelota concocted a scheme meant to confuse voters by bribing a man to enter the race who has a similar name as the republican candidate, incumbent Dan Sullivan. (This is a dirty trick used by both parties in the past.) Now Attorney General Todd Blanche, at the behest of his client/President, is proactively filing a lawsuit aiming to prevent the certification of the winner of that race if the incumbent Sullivan loses.

Obviously, the Democrats engaged slimy, dishonest and possibly illegal campaigning, and they should apologize to Alaska and the nation. However, the potential effects of such a ploy seem so inconsequential, and to litigate would be terribly insulting to the intelligence of the Alaskan voters. Are they really so stupid, so illiterate and brain-frozen that they can't read names? Don't know what incumbent means? That an S is no different than a J? Or that Daniel has six letters, Dan, three?

local.title: What kind of socialist are you?
local.summary: Anyone paying attention to state and federal politics has heard the word socialist ad nauseam ever since the 2024 elections. While on the campaign trail, President Donald Trump called Kamala Harris a socialist at every stop. Trump continues to call his political opponents socialists. During the 2026
local.body:
Anyone paying attention to state and federal politics has heard the word socialist ad nauseam ever since the 2024 elections. While on the campaign trail, President Donald Trump called Kamala Harris a socialist at every stop. Trump continues to call his political opponents socialists. During the 2026 election cycle, many Republican candidates have called their Democratic opponents socialists. In recent primaries, even Democrats have called fellow Democrats socialists and cautioned primary voters to beware.

As the phrase continues to be thrown around politically it may be helpful for individuals to examine the meaning of the word and to look at the platforms of politicians and the statements that they make to see if the candidates really are socialists. Understanding the meaning of the term may also help individuals determine if there is more to the word than just being a slur or an insult for a political opponent.

Socialism is defined as an economic and political system where the means of production — such as factories, land, machinery and natural resources — are owned or controlled collectively by the public, the community, or the state. A core characteristic of socialism is production for use where the economic focus is placed on meeting human needs such as food, housing, healthcare and education rather than generating private profit. There are different types and variations of socialism. While the United States operates fundamentally as a capitalist mixed economy, the government is filled with socialist programs that citizens make use of and benefit from every day.

Some examples of socialist programs in the U.S. government include public education, fire and police services, and our public works and infrastructure system. The roads that we drive on every day, the mail that we receive and the water and sewer systems that we use are all provided by socialism. Targeted safety net programs like Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP, Section 8 Housing and Social Security all operate under a model of collective security rather than private profit. While the U.S. military is not considered a completely socialist system, the U.S. military does operate using distinctly socialized principles. These socialist elements include state funding and ownership, universal socialized benefits for service members and their families and the lack of a free market profit motive. The U.S government doesn't profit off of our military. Defense contractors do.

local.body:
Thursday's free concert with the Army Field Band and Soldiers' Chorus was a homecoming for one member of the ensemble.

Maj. Philip Tappan, deputy commander of the United States Army Field Band, earned a master of music in Music Performance (Orchestral Conducting) from Fredonia in 2010 and a bachelor of music in Music Education in 2012.

Army Field Band's Concert Band and Soldiers' Chorus, the Army's premier touring ensembles, are comprised of a 60-piece concert band and a 24-voice chorus, featuring highly trained musicians from renowned institutions across the country.

While earning his master's degree at Fredonia, served as graduate assistant of Orchestras and Orchestral Conducting from 2008 to 2010. He returned to earn his bachelor's in Music Education and taught music in the Dunkirk City School District.

"I really enjoyed the teaching side of my graduate assistantship," Tappan said. "Teaching conducting to undergraduates was especially meaningful to me and remains one of the highlights of my time at Fredonia."

"The chamber orchestra performances were always exciting, especially when we performed early music in period style," Tappan said. "Those concerts stand out as some of my favorite musical experiences at Fredonia."

Tappan earned his Army commission in 2015 after graduating from Officer Candidate School at Fort Benning, Ga. His previous assignments include the Second Infantry Division Band and the United States Army Band "Pershing's Own," where he served as associate bandmaster; the First Cavalry Division Band as executive officer; the U.S. Army School of Music as commander and Director of Training; and the West Point Band at the United States Military Academy as deputy commander. He was deployed to Afghanistan twice, serving as officer in charge of the U.S. Forces - Afghanistan Band.

Tappan is also a composer, and his music has been performed at the Kennedy Center, the U.S. Embassy in Kabul, Afghanistan, and by professional and collegiate ensembles throughout the United States. His works span chamber, orchestral, and wind ensemble repertoire.

For the past 10 years, the Anderson-Lee Library in Silver Creek has dedicated programming each November to celebrating Native American Heritage Month. What began a decade ago as an idea shared by the late Cristine Huff and fellow library staff has grown into a much-loved community tradition. From the beginning, one of the most important parts of the program has been the opportunity to build relationships and collaborate with members of the Seneca Nation.

This year's celebration will be especially meaningful as we gather not only to honor Native American heritage and culture, but also to remember and celebrate Huff and the lasting impact she had on our library and our community.

The special one-day event will take place on Saturday, Nov. 7, at Anderson-Lee Library, 43 Main St.

The day will begin at 11 a.m. with speakers and reflections, followed by a meal at noon featuring corn soup, frybread, and strawberry drink.

At 1 p.m., the library will dedicate this year's celebration in memory of Huff. Friends, family, library patrons, and members of the community will have an opportunity to gather, share stories, and remember her and the many programs she helped bring to life over the years.

For those who knew her, this event will be a chance to celebrate the enthusiasm, kindness, and dedication she brought to the library and to the community she cared so deeply about. For those who may not have had the opportunity to know her, it will be a chance to learn about the special role she played in creating a tradition that continues to bring people together.

Please join us as we celebrate Native American Heritage Month, honor her memory, and share in the community spirit that she helped make such an important part of this annual gathering.

local.title: Trucks, treats and costumes take over Niagara Square for Halloween fun in Buffalo
local.summary: Families gathered in Niagara Square on Halloween for Buffalo’s first “Touch a Truck or Treat,” an event that brought city vehicles, costumes, candy and other activities to the heart of downtown.
local.body: Families gathered in Niagara Square on Halloween for the City of Buffalo’s first “Touch a Truck or Treat,” an event that brought city vehicles, costumes, candy and other activities to the heart of downtown.Watch story here:The free event gave children the opportunity to explore vehicles from the Buffalo Fire Department, Buffalo Police Department and Department of Public Works.“We want to make the square, which is the people’s square, we want it to be accessible, open and fun for everyone,” Gabrielle Harrington, chief of staff for Mayor Sean Ryan, told WKBW at the event.Harrington said the event also included the City of Buffalo Animal Shelter, food trucks, giveaways and a bike raffle hosted by the Delavan Grider Community Center. The event is part of an effort by Ryan’s administration to bring more activity to Niagara Square and City Hall.“Niagara Square is the people’s front yard, and we’re making it a place where Buffalo families can come together and have some fun,” Ryan said in a news release. “We’re continuing to bring new energy to the square and City Hall, and Halloween is a perfect occasion to invite everyone over.”Harrington said the Halloween event is expected to be the first of more events in the square, with the administration already considering ideas for the holiday season and next year.“I would say this is the first of many,” Harrington said. “Stay tuned. We’re going to keep bringing people down to Niagara Square.”

local.title: Donald Trump looms over New York attorney general’s race
local.summary: Attorney General Letitia James, who has been a legal thorn in the president’s side, is seeking a third term.
local.body:
Few people have gotten under President Donald Trump’s skin quite the way New York Attorney General Letitia James has.

The Democratic attorney general has long been one of the president’s chief antagonists, suing the Republican’s administration more than 80 times since she took office in 2018 while becoming a frequent target of his ire on social media and at rallies.

Now, James has made her battles with Trump a central part of her campaign to win another four years in office.

“As I travel all throughout the state of New York and even the country, individuals thank me for standing up and protecting the interest of New Yorkers,” James said in an interview with Gothamist. “They thank me for recognizing that no one is above the law and that we do not bow to kings.”

But if she’s to win on Tuesday , she’ll have to overcome a challenge from Republican Saritha Komatireddy, a former federal prosecutor who has accused James of being “obsessed with national politics,” politicizing an office that should remain apolitical.

James, the former New York City public advocate who previously served as a city councilmember from Brooklyn, first rose to the attorney general’s office in the middle of Trump’s first term in 2018.

Since then, she has become a legal thorn in the president’s side.

Her lawsuits against the Trump administration — often leading a coalition of Democratic attorneys general from other states — have targeted the president’s actions on everything from immigration enforcement to Medicaid funding to housing grants.

local.title: Two pets die in Lockport high-rise fire
local.summary: Two pets are dead Friday night following a high-rise fire in Lockport. The fire was caused by a lithium-ion battery, which was used to power an e-bike device.
local.body: Two pets are dead Friday night following a high-rise fire in Lockport.According to the City of Lockport Fire Department, just before 8:30 p.m., Lockport Fire Department responded to reports of smoke coming from a third floor apartment building on 77 Main Street.Crews found smoke visible from the exterior window but found no visible fire venting from the building. Crews determined the fire was on the fourth floor of the apartment building.LFD say there was no active fire observed but remnants of a large lithium-ion battery was smoldering in the corner of the living room.The fire was declared out within 10 minutes after arriving to the scene and crews worked on the scene for 1.5 hours. Three people suffered from non-life threatening smoke inhalation while attempting to rescue pets within the apartment. Two were taken to Lockport Hospital and one was taken to ECMC as a precaution.According to the LFD, the tenant was home at the time of the fire and attempted to rescue the animals but was overcome by smoke. Two pets were found deceased and one pet was successfully removed.The fire was caused by a lithium-ion battery, which was used to power an e-bike device.The estimated property damage was $15,000.

local.title: New York replacing decades-old unemployment system; temporary shutdown will delay payments
local.summary: New York is replacing its decades-old unemployment insurance system with a $188 million upgrade, but the transition will temporarily shut down services and delay benefit payments for people out of work.
local.body: New York is replacing its decades-old unemployment insurance system with a $188 million upgrade, but the transition will temporarily shut down services and delay benefit payments for people out of work.The New York State Department of Labor says the upgrade will begin Monday, November 2, at 5 p.m. The current system, which dates back more than 50 years, will go offline for an estimated nine to 12 days.Anyone currently collecting unemployment should make sure to file their weekly claim before 5 p.m. Monday to ensure their payments arrive as scheduled.During the shutdown, New Yorkers will not be able to file new unemployment claims, certify for weekly benefits or access and update their accounts. Phone-based services will also be unavailable."You're not allowed into the system at this point," said Labor Commissioner Roberta Reardon. "We will let you know when it's time and then you can go in and start your application. Those are the people that I'm most concerned about is somebody who's never been on unemployment and loses their job on November 5th."Reardon says the department will process claims submitted over the weekend before beginning the transition, which includes migrating more than five billion records into the new system.While payments will be delayed, the department says no one will lose benefits they are entitled to receive. People will be able to certify for those weeks once the upgraded system is available and receive their payments retroactively.People who lose their jobs during the shutdown will have to wait until the new system is online to file a claim. local.title: Buffalo business owner expands with new restaurant despite ongoing Main Street construction woes
local.summary: A Buffalo business owner is expanding - opening a new Main Street restaurant despite a longterm multimillion dollar construction project on his doorstep.
local.body: As a long-term construction project reshapes Buffalo's Main Street, some small businesses are struggling, but one owner is defying the trend by expanding.The $54 million federally funded project to allow cars to share Main Street with the train is set to continue until 2028. But signs of the strain on businesses are apparent, a bubble tea cafe closed down over the summer, along with nearby Greek restaurant Vasilis.Peter Flanagan owns lunch spot Pete's Place on the street. He tells me the construction has been a nuisance, but amidst the challenges he's decided to open a new restaurant at the former Vasilis location, next door to his current business.He's in the middle of renovating the space to become Sam's Benedict, a restaurant operated by his wife, Sam."The entire place is getting an overhaul, table chairs furniture, menu," Flanagan said.The business owner plans for the restaurant to be open for breakfast, lunch and dinner. He told me he's able to expand due to his wife's online catering business."Her reach has pulled the people in, and now our business is at capacity," Flanagan said.WATCH: Buffalo business owner expands with new restaurant despite ongoing Main Street construction woesFlanagan admitted he has some concerns about the length of the construction project but overall he's optimistic."I have high hopes for downtown. It's been dead since they first did this in the '70s when they put the rail in. Hopefully this fixes that mistake," Flanagan said. "Hopefully I can set an example for other businesses to come down here and be successful."Flanagan plans to open the new restaurant in January.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

local.title: Newfane couple warns of dangers of synthetic Kratom
local.summary: A Newfane couple is becoming advocates to warn the public about the dangers of a synthetic form of kratom after they say it claimed the life of their son.
local.body: A Newfane couple is becoming advocates to warn the public about the dangers of a synthetic form of Kratom after they say it claimed the life of their son.Jeff and Brenda Stunkel told me their 36-year-old son, Lucas, died by suicide earlier this month at their home. He had struggled with drug addiction but had been clean and sober for two-and-a-half years — until he took 7-OH, which he bought at a vape shop.The drug is a chemically altered form of Kratom, labeled "natural." It is illegal in 10 states already."I've read it's like 20 times more potent than morphine," Jeff Stunkel said. "It affects the same centers that your brain that opiates affect.”Brenda Stunkel pointed to the lack of oversight of the drug."There's no FDA regulation whatsoever, so they just do whatever they want, and they can package the pills themselves. The little packages come in with the five pills, those you can buy those packages over the internet with nothing in them, and they pop the pills in themselves," Brenda Stunkel said.The couple told me their son was at a rehab center in Niagara County trying to recover, but he called them begging for help."Please, please, please — I'm begging you to come get me," Lucas Stunkel said in a recorded phone message.Lucas came home, but shortly after — on Oct. 5 — he took his own life.Now, the couple are becoming advocates to educate the public about the dangers of this drug. Kratom is now banned in 10 states.Last year, the governor signed two landmark bills protecting New Yorkers from the harmful effects of Kratom. But then in June, state lawmakers passed a bill to ban kratom in New York. That bill remains on the governor's desk awaiting a signature.The couple is begging the governor to sign it so other families don't have to suffer.WATCH: Newfane couple warns of dangers of synthetic Kratom"I'll have to live with so many regrets of something I could have could have done different should have done different and maybe still be around that differently oh but it's that damn drug?" entertainment.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Crashes Into Tokyo Film Festival With Stars Ryunosuke Kamiki, Minami Hamabe in Tow
entertainment.summary: Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel brought costumed fans, monster figurines and rapturous applause at two sold-out festival screenings ahead of its Nov. 3 Japanese release.
entertainment.body:
The King of Monsters finally stomped his way into Japan ’s largest celebration of cinema on Sunday as Takashi Yamazaki ’s wildly anticipated Godzilla Minus Zero played to a packed pair of screenings at the Tokyo International Film Festival.

The sold-out shows easily drew the liveliest crowds of this year’s Tokyo festival — the latest Toho -backed monster epic doesn’t open commercially in Japan until Nov. 3 — with numerous die-hard kaiju fans attending in costume or carrying their own Gojira figurines into the theater. Related Stories Music Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: "It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent" Movies 'Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting' Review: Whimsical Chinese Film Explores Myth and History Through a Series of Tasty Treats

Godzilla Minus Zero is playing as the “centerpiece film” of the Tokyo festival’s programming this year, and it undoubtedly brought a welcome jolt of energy to the event as it moves through its second half. When the credits rolled on the second screening inside Hulic Hall Tokyo, the crowd erupted into uncharacteristically rapturous applause, with the always respectful but typically subdued Japanese festivalgoers all smiles and excited chatter over favorite monster moments as they poured into the autumn evening in Tokyo’s Ginza district — where much of the carnage on screen takes place.

Godzilla Minus Zero is a direct follow-up to Godzilla Minus One (2023), which Yamazaki famously wrote, directed and VFX-supervised. The film was a smash with both critics and mainstream moviegoers, making history as the highest-grossing live-action Japanese film ever in North America ($57.1 million) and later becoming the first film in the multi-decade Godzilla franchise to take home an Oscar, winning the best visual effects award despite competing in the category against Hollywood tentpoles with vastly bigger budgets.

The sequel picks up in 1949, two years after the events of Minus One , as Japan struggles to rebuild from the devastation of war and Godzilla’s attack. The Shikishima family’s hard-won peace is threatened by a new calamity, with the film also bringing iconic franchise rival King Ghidorah, the three-headed kaiju, into Yamazaki’s postwar world.

Yamazaki’s return to the helm for the follow-up has lifted expectations across the globe — and the critical response so far, along with the enthusiastic reception at home in Tokyo on Sunday, suggests he delivered. Godzilla Minus Zero premiered in September at the New York Film Festival, where The Hollywood Reporter ’s chief critic David Rooney gave it a rave , calling the film a “radioactive blast” and “a crackling kaiju epic every bit as exciting as its predecessor.” The movie currently holds a score of 92 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 52 reviews.

entertainment.title: Gracie Abrams Goes From Juliet to Romeo During ‘SNL’ Halloween Performances
entertainment.summary: The singer performed “Hit the Wall” and “Here You Come, There You Go” in costumes lifted from Baz Luhrmann’s 1996 film.
entertainment.body:
Gracie Abrams turned her Saturday Night Live return into a two-part costume change, dressing as both leads from Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet across her performances on the show’s Halloween episode Saturday (Oct. 31). Explore Gracie Abrams See latest videos, charts and news

For her first song, “ Hit the Wall ” from her third album Daughter from Hell , Abrams wore Claire Danes’ angel costume from the 1996 film and opened the performance from behind an aquarium, a nod to the movie’s fish-tank meeting scene. She returned later in the episode for “Here You Come, There You Go,” a track from the album’s deluxe edition, in Leonardo DiCaprio’s Hawaiian shirt paired with the metal sleeves from his knight’s armor. Related Valentín Elizalde's Legacy Gets a New HBO Max Docuseries & More Uplifting Moments in Latin Music Harry Styles Revives His 'X Factor' Audition Look for 'Isn't She Lovely' at Harryween Tame Impala Take On Seal's 'Kiss From a Rose' for Like A Version

It was Abrams’ second turn as SNL musical guest, following her December 2024 debut on an episode hosted by Chris Rock. Inde Navarrette hosted Saturday’s episode, her first.

The appearance comes off the biggest commercial year of Abrams’ career. Daughter from Hell , released July 17 via Interscope and produced with longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner, debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 with 124,000 equivalent album units, her first chart-topper on the all-genre list. Her 2024 album The Secret of Us had peaked at No. 2.

“ Hit the Wall ” was the album’s lead single, and Abrams has said it set the tone for everything that followed. “I just remember it being done,” she told Billboard of writing it, describing the session as almost trance-like. The song reached the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 45 on the Billboard Global 200. Her highest-charting song to date remains “That’s So True,” the deluxe-edition track from The Secret of Us that reached No. 6 on the Hot 100 and became her first top 10 there.

Abrams takes Daughter from Hell on the road in December. Her Look at My Life Tour opens Dec. 2 in Denver and runs into May 2027, including four nights at London’s O2 Arena.

entertainment.title: ‘SNL’ Parodies Nicki Minaj After Her Trump Rally Appearance
entertainment.summary: Saidah Belo-Osagie played the rapper days after Minaj joined Trump at a Michigan rally.
entertainment.body:
Saturday Night Live turned its Halloween cold open on Saturday (Oct. 31) into a send-up of Nicki Minaj ’s support for President Donald Trump, a week after the rapper joined him on the campaign trail . Explore Nicki Minaj See latest videos, charts and news

Cast member Saidah Belo-Osagie played Minaj, bursting into the sketch near its end as James Austin Johnson’s Trump praised her loyalty to his movement. “Trump’s out here killing it,” Belo-Osagie’s Minaj declared, “and by it, I mean my career.” The sketch also cast her as Trump’s next choice for White House press secretary. Related Atlanta Gridiron Classic 2026: Here's Where to Watch Florida Gators vs. Georgia Bulldogs Live Online Free Joe Budden Makes 'Law & Order' Cameo as a Rapper Named Big Switty The 36 Best Christmas Gifts to Shop Online in 2026

The parody drew directly on Minaj’s appearance at Trump’s Oct. 25 rally in Port Huron, Michigan, where she traveled with him on Air Force One and backed Republican candidates Mike Rogers and John James ahead of Tuesday’s (Nov. 3) midterm elections. During the rally, Trump invited Minaj to stand before the crowd and commented on her appearance , a moment the sketch played on with Johnson’s Trump making a string of jokes about the subject.

The press secretary gag also had a real-world source. A Trump staffer floated Minaj for the role during the Air Force One trip, and Trump later told The Benny Show it was “a good idea,” adding, “I’m gonna think about that.” Minaj has also said she is “not going anywhere” after Trump called her his “favorite.”

The cold open was framed as a ride through a budget Halloween haunted attraction, with Grace Reiter and Jeremy Culhane as a couple on a date and Kenan Thompson as a Grim Reaper guide. Tom Hanks then appeared as David S. Pumpkins, the oddball character he introduced on the show in 2016, backed by his dancing skeleton sidekicks Mikey Day and former cast member Bobby Moynihan, in what the sketch itself called the character’s third outing.

Before the bit could get going, Johnson’s Trump froze the scene and cut it short. “I’ll save you four minutes: he keeps popping up and confusing people on the ride. The end,” he told the audience, before comparing himself to Pumpkins: “We both appeared in 2016, we’re both very loud, very orange.” He went on to complain about Republican polling ahead of the midterms before Belo-Osagie’s Minaj made her entrance.

entertainment.body:
Logo text Inde Navarrette made her Saturday Night Live hosting debut on the show’s Halloween episode, and kicked things off with a dig at the most recent host of the late night series.

The actress began her monologue by referencing her star-making role in Obsession : “You probably know me from the movie Obsession . People ask me if I’m anything like my character Nikki, and I’m like, no. No, no, don’t do that.”

“But the thing is, I’m nothing like my character in Obsession . Like, my boyfriend is here tonight to support me,” she said, as the camera panned over to her boyfriend, Nick Aiello, duck-taped in the audience. “We have such a chill relationship, right?” Related Stories News LAPD Arrests Two for Murder of Christina Downer, Sister to 'SNL' Writer Jimmy Fowlie Movies Santa Barbara Film Fest: Inde Navarrette, Jaafar Jackson Among Eight Tapped for Virtuoso Awards

Navarrette went on to discuss how she’ll be next portraying Rogue in Marvel Studios’ X-Men reboot . The character preps requires a lot of working out, she noted. “I can’t believe I’m saying this, but I’m gonna be in a Marvel movie. I know it’s really important for Marvel that you get really fit, so I’ve been working out a lot.”

“So every morning, I put on my little whore outfit, and I hit the gym,” she said, in a callback to Shane Gillis’ controversial monologue on the most recent episode of SNL on Oct. 10.

During his SNL appearance, he said at the top of the episode, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now. Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. You’ve seen the shorts? They’re those neon, like, artificial vape-colored [shorts], and the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look, you’re not allowed to look!”

Continuing with her monologue, Navarrette invited the SNL cast to the stage to show off their Halloween costumes “since none of the cast could go out tonight.” Marcello Hernandez appeared as “a sexy TSA agent,” as Kam Patterson portrayed Elizabeth Holmes.

Jeremy Culhane also joined, using his time during Navarrette’s monologue as an audition for Jake Schreier’s upcoming X-Men movie.

entertainment.title: Heidi Klum Reveals This Year’s (Very Bloody) Halloween Costume
entertainment.summary: The star transformed into a severed hand for her famous Halloween party on Saturday night.
entertainment.body:
It wouldn’t be Halloween without Heidi Klum , as the star revealed yet another jaw-dropping costume at her signature party on Saturday night.

The Queen of Halloween, as she has become known, celebrated the 25th anniversary of her NYC Halloween party this year, and Klum took it to the next level as she showed up as a severed hand.

She arrived in a truck covered in red “danger” sings, helped to the ground by actors in yellow hazmat suits. Klum’s elaborate costume includes a bloody wrist and her head at the center of the hand, with fingers featuring rings and a fresh manicure; she revealed in red carpet interviews it was an intricate recreation of her own hand. The star appeared without husband Tom Kaulitz, who has dressed up alongside her in recent years. Related Stories Lifestyle Best Celebrity Halloween Costumes 2026: Paris Hilton as Britney Spears, Lisa Rinna as Kylie Jenner and More Movies 'Halloween' Star Danielle Harris Opens Up About Her Career and Personal Trauma in New Feature Documentary (Exclusive)

Klum is hosting the event, presented by Apothic and Butterfinger, at Cathédrale Restaurant at Moxy East Village. The party has become one of Spooky Season’s most iconic events, as Klum always turns up in an elaborate look — in recent years, she’s transformed into Medusa , E.T. , a peacock, Fiona from Shrek , Jessica Rabbit and famously, a worm .

The supermodel has been teasing glimpses at her costume on her Instagram, teasing her transformation all day long while asking her followers to submit their guesses on what she would become. Klum collaborates on her costumes with special effects makeup designer Mike Marino, who won an Emmy for his work on The Penguin . Marino revealed in a recent interview that “this costume this year is one of the most elaborate costumes ever made. It’s so difficult to do and just the complication of it is really challenging.”

Klum herself promised earlier this year to People that her look was “very, very bloody” and “goes very well with red wine;” she has partnered with Apothic Wines on limited-edition Apothic x Heidi Klum Type ‘A’ Blood Bags, a Halloween collectible inspired by the look of blood bags that were also served at the party.

entertainment.title: ‘Green Room’ Director Recalls How Patrick Stewart “Saved” Movie From Being Scrapped
entertainment.summary: Ahead of a screening of the film on Friday, Jeremy Saulnier recounted how 'Green Room' was "close to shutting down" when the sci-fi icon, "out of the blue, expressed interest in the project."
entertainment.body:
Logo text Green Room director Jeremy Saulnier paid tribute to Patrick Stewart ahead of a Los Angeles screening of the film on Friday, recalling how the sci-fi icon “just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us.”

Celebrating the film’s 10th anniversary, Saulnier addressed the crowd and noted Stewart’s death at 86.

“Who’s sad as fuck we lost Patrick Stewart yesterday? Me,” he said in a video posted on the Film Updates X account. “I came here to shamelessly promote Slayground , but instead, I’m just gonna celebrate Patrick Stewart. He had no business doing this movie. He every option to do otherwise.” Related Stories Movies Before 'Star Trek,' Patrick Stewart Proved His Sci-Fi Chops in 'Dune' Critic's Appreciation Patrick Stewart's Career Was a Rare and Thrilling Marriage of the Prestigious and the Populist

The director remembered how production on Green Room was “at the point of no return, building sets, and under the gun without Darcy,” noting that the lead character of Darcy Banker had not yet been cast. However, that’s when the Star Trek star came in.

“We’re fucked, and we were close to shutting down. And Patrick Stewart, out of the blue, sort of expressed interest in the project,” Saulnier said. “And in a whirlwind, about a week later, I was on the phone with him. I left the stage [thinking,] ‘Maybe we’re gonna have to break down the sets and shut the whole movie down.’ Instead, this dude came out of nowhere, from way above our sort of zone, and just swooped down, nosedived into our cruddy ass movie and saved us, and said yes. And the movie was instantly greenlit.”

“We moved forward, and I thank him for just taking that leap and making Green Room a thing,” he added. “Patrick Stewart is why I still can make movies. He saved the day. Too good to be true.”

The Rebel Ridge director remembered Stewart as a “fucking sweetheart, true gentleman, [who was a] very kind leader to our whole cast.” He also shared a story about how one day, the actor came to him and said he “wanted to add a little something” to a scene.

“I was like, ‘What is it, Patrick?’ He’s like, ‘Well, during this one part of the scene, when the camera’s coming through there, I’d like to say, fuck!’ And I was like, ‘And?’ ‘Just fuck.’ I was like. ‘Permission granted, sir,’” Saulnier recounted. “And I just knew that he was completely aligned with the film, its aesthetic, its intentions and with me as a filmmaker, and it was just this lovely, lovely thing.”

entertainment.title: Trump Lawsuit Against Wall Street Journal Over Epstein Story Dismissed by Judge
entertainment.summary: U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law.
entertainment.body:
Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump ’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein .

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal ’s investigative reporting. Related Stories TV Bill Maher Responds to Trump's 1,318-Word Social Rant: "He Went Off on Me Like Kelly Clarkson in a Toy Store" Music Canadian Rock Icon Bryan Adams Takes Aim at Trump, Says His Protest Song Gets Standing Ovations in Red States (Exclusive)

When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.

The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.

Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists.

The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.

The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.

The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.

entertainment.title: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Director Taika Waititi Calls Critics “Sad Lost Souls” Over Negative Reviews
entertainment.summary: Set in a dystopian future, the film stars Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams.
entertainment.body:
Klara and the Sun director Taika Waititi is pushing back against negative reviews of his latest film.

Waititi took to Instagram on Saturday, where he shared the film’s poster and highlighted the contrast between its audience and critics scores on Rotten Tomatoes. The poster shows that the film has a 78 percent audience score, compared to a 28 percent critics score.

“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people,” Waititi wrote in his Instagram caption. “So this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit . Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.” Related Stories Movies Justin Long Joins Jenna Ortega, Rose Byrne in Drama 'Nasty' (Exclusive) Movies 'Clayface' Rolls to $24M Box Office Opening as 'You Can See Everything' Shines in Second Weekend

The film, which opened in theaters last week, earned an estimated $725,000 in its opening weekend at the box office and debuted outside the top 10. It opened in 880 North American theaters. As of publication, the film grossed approximately $1.7 million worldwide.

Adapted from Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel of the same name, Klara and the Sun is set in a dystopian future and follows an obsolete companion android who attempts to bond with her new owner, Josie, a young girl dealing with an illness. Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams star in the film.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter at the film’s New York premiere earlier this month, Waititi also shared his thoughts on artificial intelligence, which plays a central role in the film’s premise of AI companions.

“There’s a big discussion about AI coming in: Will people use it? How much will they use it? I know it’s probably inevitable that we end up using it in our industry, but as long as it’s used by humans as a tool, as opposed to a replacement — I don’t want to replace humans. I want to work with them,” he said.

entertainment.title: Deep Purple’s Ian Gillan Hospitalized Following Medical Emergency, Two Shows Postponed
entertainment.summary: The 81-year-old singer was scheduled to perform in Germany over the weekend.
entertainment.body:
Deep Purple frontman Ian Gillan has been hospitalized following a medical emergency, forcing the legendary British rock band to postpone two concerts in Germany.

In a statement shared on Instagram Saturday (Oct. 31), Deep Purple announced “with great disappointment” that its concert at QI Arena in Leipzig that evening, as well as its upcoming performance at Sporthalle Hamburg, had been postponed.

“This comes as a result of a medical emergency involving Ian Gillan, which has resulted in his current hospitalisation,” wrote the band, which also features guitarist Simon McBride, bassist Roger Glover, drummer Ian Paice and keyboardist Don Airey.

Deep Purple did not provide further details about Gillan’s condition or indicate when he might be released from the hospital.

“We understand that this announcement comes at short notice and share the disappointment of all our wonderful fans that we are unable to perform in Leipzig and Hamburg.”

The band added that it is working to find a “suitable time to reschedule” both concerts. Tickets purchased for the original dates will remain valid for the rescheduled performances.

Deep Purple has been on the road for its SPLAT! world tour since late summer, with additional dates scheduled across Europe, the United Kingdom, South America and Mexico through late December.

Gillan has served as Deep Purple’s lead vocalist during multiple stints, first joining the band in 1969. He is the voice behind some of the British rock group’s best-known hits such as “Smoke on the Water”and “Highway Star.”
